newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso proposes talks with Brazil land militants.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso proposes talks with Brazil land militants.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Tuesday introduced measures to speed land reform and offered an olive branch to the militant Landless Movement (MST), his sharpest critic on the land ownership issue.

"No one can be so arrogant to claim they have the absolute truth because absolute truth does not exist," Cardoso said at a ceremony attended by MST representatives, the first formal meeting between the government and the group since August 1996.
Officials cut off talks with the MST last year after the group refused to give up its tactic of organizing massive invasions of unused farmland by landless peasants.
About 1,000 MST members are marching from three points in Brazil for a demonstration in the capital Brasilia on April 17, the first anniversary of a massacre of 19 landless protesters by police.

Cardoso praised the march as "positive" and said the government would hold a "Brazilian forum, capable of allowing more dialogue, capable of allowing the forces which are opposed over this issue to participate and to participate actively."
Brazil has one of the world's most unequal land ownership ratios, with one percent of landowners holding about 45 percent of farmland, according to estimates by the Catholic Church.
The government has been disappropriating large unused estates and allocating them to landless families. It says it is on target for its aim of settling 280,000 families in four years.
But a recent poll found 85 percent of Brazilians supported the MST's land occupations, as long as they do not use violence.

In a weekly radio address broadcast earlier on Tuesday, Cardoso said a task force comprising several ministries would speed up installation of basic infrastructure in settlements, including construction of more than 1,000 schools by the end of 1998.

The president also announced what he said was a "revolutionary" plan to decentralize land reform, giving states and municipalities the power to use their properties or buy farms and turn them over to landless families.
Another new measure would enable landless workers to take out bank loans to buy land, sidestepping the bureaucracy of the government's land reform program, Cardoso said.

"This government is settling four times as many families as its predecessors," Cardoso said in the address. "And we want to do more than settle, we want the settlements to work and the settlers to become productive farmers quickly."
